text: You've already pulled alerts out of Defender XDR and Sentinel through their own portals. The Microsoft Graph Security API gives you one programmatic surface instead -- a single schema that returns alerts and incidents from Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Identity, Defender for Office 365, Defender for Cloud Apps, and Sentinel, all normalized the same way. One parser, not five.

Two resources matter most for automation. Alerts v2 gives you individual alerts, each with a severity, a status, a classification, and an evidence array describing exactly what was observed. Incidents groups one or more correlated alerts into a single case, with its own severity, status, determination, and assigned owner. Evidence is the real payoff -- device, user, IP, file, and process artifacts, all tagged consistently no matter which product generated the alert.

Script-driven access uses an app-only token, not a signed-in user. You register an app in Azure AD, grant it application permissions like SecurityAlert dot Read dot All with admin consent, and generate a client secret. MSAL exchanges that secret for an access token through the client credentials flow. Notice the scope is always dot default -- that tells Azure AD to issue a token for whatever permissions were already granted, rather than listing individual scopes yourself.

With a bearer token in hand, alerts and incidents are plain REST calls, and Graph supports OData query options -- filter narrows results on the server instead of pulling everything and filtering in Python afterward. Graph never returns more than one page at a time, so the while loop keeps following odata next link, the cursor telling you whether more results exist, until it comes back empty and you know you've pulled everything that matched.

The evidence array is where the unified schema really pays off. Each entry carries an odata type discriminator, so a script can loop through evidence, check whether an entry is IP evidence, user evidence, or device evidence, and pull out exactly the field it needs -- without caring which underlying product generated the alert in the first place. That loop-and-branch pattern is one you'll reuse constantly once you start correlating findings across tools.

That's the unified Graph Security API: one schema, app-only authentication through MSAL, filtered and paginated REST queries, and a consistent evidence structure underneath every alert. Next lesson, you'll go one level deeper into Sentinel specifically -- running real KQL queries against a Log Analytics workspace, and calling the Sentinel incidents REST API directly from Python.
